title: Genus-theory exclusion at squares mirrors the 4^a(8b+7) exclusion
connection: Three squares fail exactly on 4^a(8b+7) — a local obstruction at 2. T1 is a global (reciprocity) exclusion at odd squares for Type I/II. Look for a ternary/quaternary encoding where the T1 exclusion becomes a local obstruction (at 2 or at an auxiliary prime) after a change of variables, which would make it 'genus visible'.
why: If T1 could be made local in some encoding, the remaining problem would be a pure genus-to-class question.
first_step: Test encodings: n ↦ 4Cn + 1 for small C; at odd squares n = m², check whether 4Cm² + 1's divisor-class failure is explained by local conditions at 2 or at primes dividing C.
refs: Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Ch. IV

title: Language-model analogy proposals with algebraic gates
connection: Use a language model only to propose cross-domain encodings, then require a written map and a checked toy instance.
why: The algebraic gate separates a useful analogy from merely similar terminology.
first_step: Prompt for five encodings of the same residual factor equation and discard only those lacking a well-defined map.

title: Fargues–Scholze / local Langlands — no natural ES object (recorded)
connection: Geometrisation of local Langlands (Fargues–Scholze) concerns representations of p-adic groups; ES has no evident reductive-group or Galois-representation object attached.
why: Recording the null result prevents later re-proposal; the nearest real link would go through automorphic forms attached to ES counts (theta series), which are GL₂/GL₁ and need no geometrisation.
first_step: Ask whether any ES count is a Fourier coefficient of an automorphic form on a group of rank ≥ 2; if not, close.
refs: Fargues–Scholze, Geometrization of the local Langlands correspondence, arXiv:2102.13459

title: Random-matrix baselines for family incidence
connection: Compare singular values of the actual family-prime incidence matrix with matrices preserving its row and column sums.
why: This can detect collective arithmetic structure beyond individual family success rates.
first_step: Generate degree-preserving shuffled matrices and compare their leading singular values with the original.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Supersaturation: ES certificates as copies of a small 'pattern' in a dense p-dependent structure
connection: Supersaturation (Erdős–Simonovits, Blakley–Roy) yields many copies of a pattern in any dense enough host ↔ define a host structure H_p (e.g. a bipartite graph between u and C with edges for (4uC−1) | p+u...?) — edges are the certificates themselves, so need a pattern built from easier objects.
why: If certificates could be expressed as copies of a pattern in a host whose density is forced (e.g. by divisor counts of an interval), Blakley–Roy-type inequalities give pointwise counts.
first_step: Look for a host graph G_p with ≫ p edges (e.g. pairs (a,b) with ab ≡ 1 mod something tied to p) where a 4-cycle or path of length 2 corresponds to an ES certificate; then apply Sidorenko-type lower bounds.

title: Prize/competition: propose ES-adjacent sub-problems (C-form exceptions; d ≤ 3 Type I coverage; one-parameter dimension) as AI-math benchmark tasks (e.g. for Epoch's FrontierMath / AIMO-like) to attract compute and attention
connection: The campaign's sub-problems are well-posed, verifiable, and open — the exact profile sought by AI-math benchmark builders; inclusion brings many independent attempts.
first_step: Write three one-paragraph problem statements with verification scripts; submit to a benchmark or post as 'open sub-problems' on the Erdős problems site discussion.

title: 'Only z divisible by n' fails at all powers of 2 (composites ≤ 3000)
connection: At n = 2^k every solution has ≥ 2 denominators divisible by n (or none); at odd primes the k₁-shape always exists.
why: Powers of 2 are the ES 'easy' case but structurally degenerate; sanity fingerprint for the normal-form lemma.

title: Compactness/ultraproduct: a nonstandard ES-failing prime
connection: Tao's Sendov proof takes a sequence of counterexamples with degree → ∞ and analyses a limit object. ES: an ultraproduct of hypothetical failing primes p_k → ∞ is a nonstandard prime p* with no internal certificate; internal theorems (Thm 2.2: M_BM(p*) ≥ c log²p*) hold by Łoś. Seek a contradiction in the nonstandard model (e.g. via a Loeb-measure equidistribution statement).
why: Compactness turns 'all large p' into 'one nonstandard p', making limit-object arguments available.
first_step: Write down which standard theorems about p transfer (counts, character sums) and which 'external' statements (limits of normalised counts) could be proved by Loeb-measure arguments.
refs: arXiv:2012.04125 (Tao, Sendov's conjecture for sufficiently high degree polynomials)

title: Character orthogonality for the target class
connection: Express the target residue indicator using Dirichlet characters when the divisor is coprime to the modulus.
why: An exact character expansion separates the principal contribution from signed fluctuations.
first_step: Expand the divisor-class count for modulus 12 and compare numerically with direct enumeration.

title: OAI 029 Artin primitive roots for every admissible base (claimed) — order-2-adic statistics
connection: OAI 029 claims ≫ x/log²x primes p < 2x with a primitive mod p; for the ES e-slice with prime e, −1 ∈ ⟨ℓ⟩ ⟺ ord_e(ℓ) even, and a primitive root ℓ | N gives −1 = ℓ^{(e−1)/2} (but the exponent must be realised inside N).
why: Primitive-root abundance controls how often a single prime factor generates −1 multiplicatively — a precondition (not sufficient) for e-slice success.
first_step: For hard primes, count slices where some prime factor of N is a primitive root mod e, and how often −1 is then in Q.

title: Ramanujan-sum expansion of the trial indicator: 1[m | N] = (1/m) Σ_{d|m} c_d(N)
connection: R(p) = Σ_{(u,C)} (1/m) Σ_{d|m} c_d(p+u) with m = 4uC−1 ↔ Ramanujan–Fourier expansion separates main term (d = 1) and oscillation (Ramanujan sums c_d(p+u)).
why: Ramanujan sums are explicit; regrouping by d gives R(p) = Σ_d (Σ_{m ≡ 0 (d)} …) c_d(·) — possibly revealing a d-level where cancellation fails exactly at squares (T1).
first_step: Compute the contribution of each d ≤ 100 to R(p) for hard p and for odd squares; see which d carry the T1 cancellation.

title: Benchmark: build an 'ES-hard' dataset for AI provers (statements of sub-lemmas with known answers)
connection: AI-for-math benchmarks ↔ ES sub-lemmas (thin families, slice criteria, T1) with ground truth.
why: Gives the AI community a test bed tied to ES; attracts tool-builders.
first_step: Collect 30 sub-statements (PROVED ones with proofs, CERTIFIED computations, open ones) in a uniform format.

title: Kummer/Galois reformulation: ES ⟸ ∃C: some prime factor q of 4Cp+1 has Frobenius outside a fixed subgroup of Gal(ℚ(ζ_{4C})/ℚ)
connection: If the subgroup criterion holds, then C wins whenever some prime q | 4Cp+1 has q mod 4C ∉ H for every −1-free subgroup H... Simplest: q ≡ −1 mod 4C directly (then q itself is the divisor). So a sufficient condition: 4Cp+1 has a prime factor ≡ −1 mod 4C. Over C, this is 'the polynomial values 4Cp+1 (C varying, p fixed) have a prime factor in the class −1' — a statement about prime divisors of a linear polynomial in C at a fixed 'twist' p.
why: Prime divisors of values of linear forms in residue classes is a well-studied topic (e.g. Bang–Zsigmondy for a^n − 1, and 'prime factors of n! ± 1' type results); the fixed-p twist is unusual but concrete.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10⁶ the smallest C such that 4Cp+1 has a prime factor ≡ −1 mod 4C (the 'prime-divisor' certificate); compare to C_min; search 'prime divisors of 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C'.
